UK air traffic control provider boss given one week to deliver report into flight chaos
Gwyn TophamandMark Sweney
The head of the UK air traffic control provider Nats has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure that has disrupted thousands of flights in the UK and across Europe since Tuesday.
Downing Street said the government still had confidence in Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe, who was summoned to meet the UK transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, on Wednesday morning as the number of flight cancellations passed 2,000.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted and delayed, with many stuck on grounded planes for many hours as the incident unravelled. Other passengers were stranded overnight at airports in the UK and abroad.
Alexander raised “significant concerns” with Rolfe, according to the prime minister’s official spokesperson, who told reporters: “She’s asked him to carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn’t happen again.”
They added: “It’s self-evident that she wants answers and the full investigation to be reported back in a week’s time, and she’s got confidence in him to deliver that.”
Pressed on whether the government’s confidence in the head of air traffic control was conditional on the investigation, the spokesperson replied: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with the investigation, which will report in a week’s time.”
Airlines including Ryanair and WizzAir have called for Rolfe to resign or be sacked by Alexander.
EU grants Spain €115m in aid for Ceuta, border security
Meanwhile, the European Union said it was granting Spain €115m in emergency aid to help bolster border security and assist returns after the massive migrant rush into the north African exclave, AFP reported.
“The situation in Ceuta has put pressure on our external borders. Our message remains clear: we are committed to combat illegal migration and ensure the swift return of those who remain illegally in Ceuta,” said European Commission vice-president Henna Virkkunen.
German chancellor accuses far-right AfD party of seeking ‘ethnic cleansing’
And if you missed our earlier coverage of Friedrich Merz’s fiery debate with AfD’s leader Alice Weidel (10:05, 10:21),we have this report by our Berlin correspondent, Deborah Cole.
“Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.
In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.
“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.
In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.
“If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”
He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.
Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living.
He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering bid to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.”
Germany's Pistorius warns against 'real, serious, acute' threat from Russia and criticises 'treasonous' AfD
Meanwhile, German defence minister Boris Pistorius is speaking in the Bundestag, outlining why Germany needs to ramp up its defence spending to counter the emerging threat from Russia.
He says the proposed spending is needed to deliver on the pledge to keep the country safe, despite some criticism based on “very simplistic approach” of “populist” comparisons against schools, roads, or hospitals.
“A strong, capable Bundeswehr and a united, capable Nato are essential if we are to truly protect and preserve our achievements and our way of life. Without security, nothing else matters,” he says.
He says the Russian threat Germany and Europe more broadly is “real, serious and acute,” as demonstrated by the recent attempted drone attack in Leipzig, as well as other incidents including an armed Russian fighter jet in Estonian airspace and drone incidents elsewhere.
“Russia is attempting to spy on, influence, intimidate, and destabilize our societies – and, above all, to sow uncertainty among the public. And this represents a new level of threat. Moscow is increasingly willing to accept the risk of escalation.”
He says Russia is “massively ramping up” its defence spending, a clear “threat” against Europe.
Without willing to disclose too much, Pistorius adds:
“Why, after all, did CIA Director Radcliffe travel to Moscow just under two weeks ago? Certainly not to buy matryoshka dolls or go to the ballet.”
“And the only ones … who deny it, who call him a friend … who want to pull out Nato and jeopardise the security of us all, they are sitting right there – that is the AfD,” he says, adding that the party’s links with Russia are “treasonous.”
“You need to realize that these are the very people ready to hand us over to Putin tomorrow,” he warns.
Coffin of King Harald being moved to the royal mausoleum at Akershus Fortress
Back in Oslo, the funeral procession with the coffin of Norway’s King Harald V is now again on the move.
After a funeral service at the Oslo Cathedral, the coffin is now being moved towards Akershus Fortress, where the late monarch will be buried in the royal mausoleum, next to his parents and grandparents.
After the ceremony at the cathedral, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a “missing man” formation, their tribute to the king.
A senior politician in the Social Democratic party, Merz’s coalition partners, Dirk Wiese, condemned Trump’s social media comments as “interference” with German politics, and calling them “unacceptable.”

EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.
In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.
National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.
Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.
The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.
“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.
Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities.
“It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the country’s president Aleksandar Vučić dissolved parliament and announced snap elections for next month as he seeks to extend his hold on power by running for prime minister.
Reuters reported that Vučić, a populist who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by the collapse of a railway station awning in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
At least 20 injured after passenger train crashes with truck in Poland
At least 20 people have been injured, four of them seriously, after an InterCity passenger train struck a truck at a level crossing in Poland and derailed.
Poland’s railway operator, PKP Intercity, said 120 people were on board at the time of the crash.
Russia hopes to see restarted peace talks with Ukraine, says Europe 'harming itself' by cutting off Russian gas
Russia hopes that peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, will resume in the near future, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in comments reported by Reuters.
No such direct talks have taken place since February.
But the Kremlin will not publicly discuss potential elements of a possible peace settlement, Peskov added.
He was speaking after Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump had a telephone call on Tuesday to discuss prospects for ending the war.
Peskov also said that European countries have found themselves in a difficult position amid rising gas prices, and that they could buy gas at cheaper prices from Russia.
European natural gas prices have soared amid the war in Iran, hitting their highest level last week since late 2022, when the start of the Ukraine conflict prompted Europe to cut off Russian pipeline gas.
Peskov said Europe was harming itself by buying expensive gas at spot prices as opposed to the more affordable Russian option, and suggested that the controversial Nord Stream pipeline could be restarted soon.
Kremlin’s spokesperson also confirmed that Russia would respond to Hungary’s decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats from Budapest.

articles.title: Kyiv Warns Russia Will “Test” New Long-Range Missile Against Western Ukraine

Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new, currently unnamed ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers (500 miles) by the end of 2026 and could attack western Ukraine as trials of the system.
Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitsky, deputy head of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) delivered the assessment during a recent meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council.

“According to our estimates, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers by the end of this year,” Skibitsky said.
Ukrainian intelligence believes Russia could attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine during as part of its testing regime.
Skibitsky said Russia was increasing the intensity of missile and drone attacks against Ukraine in an effort to trigger a social and economic crisis. Moscow is also seeking to increase its production of ballistic missiles and extend their range, he said.
Skibitsky urged Ukraine’s partners to strengthen sanctions against Russia and restrict its access to foreign components used in the production of long-range weapons.
Intelligence says Russian losses exceeded recruitment
Skibitsky also said Russia lost about 43,000 military personnel in August while recruiting around 39,000 people into its armed forces.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Russian General Staff believes intensified mobilization is the only way Moscow can achieve its main military objectives.

“Russia has not abandoned its strategic goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood and is waging a war of attrition despite heavy losses,” Skibitsky said.
He said those objectives included the complete occupation of Ukraine’s Donbas region and attempts to secure the strategic initiative on the battlefield.
Russia intends to mobilize about 600,000 people during 2026 and 2027, with half of that number expected to be recruited by the end of this year, according to HUR’s assessment.
Belarus could support hybrid operations
Skibitsky said Russia’s broader plans also included attempts to blockade the Black Sea and draw Belarus into the war against Ukraine alongside hybrid operations targeting NATO.
However, Ukrainian intelligence has not detected signs that Belarus is currently preparing offensive military formations on its territory, he said.
“At present, we do not see real indicators of preparations for strike groups on Belarusian territory, but we remember January and February 2022,” Skibitsky said.
He identified domestic political risks, limited military capabilities and possible economic problems as the primary factors discouraging Belarus from directly entering the war.
However, HUR considers it likely that Belarus will continue supporting Russian hybrid activities, including allowing its territory to be used to increase pressure along NATO’s borders and to intensify information and psychological operations.
Skibitsky said Russia remained a threat to both Ukraine and Europe. He thanked partner countries for their support and again called for stronger sanctions to deprive Moscow of foreign components used in weapons targeting Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine reveals ‘game changer’ RAM-2X strike drone
articles.body:
Ukrainian defence manufacturer UKRSPECSYSTEMS has publicly identified itself as the maker of the RAM-2X precision-strike uncrewed aerial system, revealing a weapon the firm says has already been used extensively in combat and produced at scale rather than a new developmental design.
The company unveiled RAM-2X under its own name at the MSPO defence exhibition in Kielce, Poland, on 8 September, after previously withholding its involvement for Ukrainian security reasons. UKRSPECSYSTEMS says the system has been manufactured and employed operationally at large scale by Ukraine’s Defence Forces.
Speaking to the UK Defence Journal ahead of the announcement, Rory Chamberlain, Managing Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS UK, said the company had wanted to discuss the system publicly for some time but had been prevented from doing so by Ukrainian security considerations.
He said those restrictions had now reduced sufficiently to allow UKRSPECSYSTEMS to identify itself as the manufacturer and begin discussing a capability that had previously remained largely hidden behind operational footage and battlefield reports.
Chamberlain told us RAM-2X became fully operational in 2024. Asked what the company meant when it described the system as being used at large scale, he would not provide an exact figure but said the scale was already in the “tens of thousands”, adding that this was a low estimate. On the company’s account, RAM-2X has already been developed, adapted and employed through several years of high-intensity war before the company has been able to put its name publicly alongside the system.
In its formal announcement, Chamberlain said: “RAM-2X isn’t new to the battlefield; what is new today is that we can finally talk about it publicly. It has been developed through combat and continuously improved using feedback from the Ukrainian units operating it.
“What matters is not simply the range or performance of an individual aircraft. RAM-2X demonstrates a different approach to precision strike: matching the effector to the target and generating military effect at a price and scale that can be sustained in war. And when RAM-2X is connected with SHARK-M, the result is much more than two drones. Persistent reconnaissance and precision strike become part of the same operational system – finding, tracking and engaging demanding targets at depth.”
Combat footage opened to public scrutiny
Alongside the reveal, UKRSPECSYSTEMS has opened what it calls the X-Archive, a collection of combat footage the company says was supplied by Ukrainian military units operating RAM systems and cleared for public release. The initial material concentrates on Russian air-defence equipment, with the company saying RAM systems have been credited with strikes against more than 450 air-defence-class targets.
That figure is the company’s own and refers to RAM systems collectively, so it should not be read as confirmation that RAM-2X alone conducted all 450 engagements. UKRSPECSYSTEMS is progressively releasing footage that it says can now be publicly associated with the RAM family after previously circulating without attribution.
Chamberlain also gave the UK Defence Journal additional detail on how the desired effect against such targets has changed during the war. He said RAM-2X had moved from an approach in which attacks could seek a mission kill, disabling a system sufficiently to take it out of the fight, towards one where Ukrainian forces increasingly sought complete destruction. The reason, he explained, was that equipment left damaged on the battlefield could subsequently be used as a decoy, changing the Ukrainian concept of operations.
Chamberlain said: “So now we aim for total kill on all the systems.”
He said SHARK reconnaissance aircraft remain over the area to provide rapid battle damage assessment after an engagement, allowing the unit to establish the effect of the strike.
Dmytro Khasapov, General Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS, said: “This is not the beginning of RAM-2X’s story. It is simply the first time we are able to tell that story publicly. RAM-2X was developed in Ukraine, through combat, against real targets and in one of the most demanding electronic-warfare environments in the world. When we say combat-proven, we mean evidence, not a marketing claim. That is why, alongside RAM-2X, we are opening the X-Archive so people can see declassified evidence of the system at work.”
Up to 180km range with a 3.5kg warhead
RAM-2X is intended for precision strikes against high-value targets at operational-tactical depth. UKRSPECSYSTEMS gives the aircraft a range of up to 180 kilometres, endurance exceeding two hours and a 3.5kg warhead. According to the company, the system incorporates automatic target lock and tracking, while available options include optical navigation for operations where satellite navigation is denied and AI-based object recognition.
That electronic-warfare resilience is particularly important in Ukraine, where satellite navigation, control links and communications are routinely subjected to jamming and other forms of interference.
Rather than presenting RAM-2X as an isolated aircraft, UKRSPECSYSTEMS is positioning it as part of a broader reconnaissance-strike architecture connecting sensors, communications, ground control, software and effectors.
SHARK-M links reconnaissance directly to strike
A central element of that architecture is the relationship between RAM-2X and the company’s SHARK-M reconnaissance UAS, a pairing UKRSPECSYSTEMS calls the “Killer Duo”. SHARK-M is used for persistent reconnaissance and targeting, while RAM-2X provides the strike component. The company says the reconnaissance aircraft can also act as a communications relay in heavily contested electronic-warfare conditions.
Asked how closely the two aircraft are integrated, Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that information is shared automatically between the systems. That matters particularly for attacks at depth because targets may move between initial detection and the arrival of the strike aircraft. Persistent surveillance, he said, allows the target to remain under observation throughout that process.
Chamberlain said: “They’re all automatically shared. So it’s that full integration, and you have to understand that in Ukraine, your targets are often moving, and when we are looking at the deep strike as well, and the time onto target, it’s important that you have ISR with persistence there.”
The company’s wider argument is that shortening the connection between finding a target and attacking it can be as important as the performance of the strike aircraft itself.
Battlefield imagery used to train target recognition
Chamberlain also explained how UKRSPECSYSTEMS is using years of reconnaissance imagery to develop the AI-based object recognition offered with RAM-2X. He said the company’s ISR systems have been observing Russian targets since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, building up imagery as equipment, camouflage and operating practices have changed.
That includes seeing targets in low light, partly hidden by vegetation or otherwise presented differently from a clean reference image. Chamberlain said this material is used to train recognition systems across RAM-2X, SHARK and the company’s wider portfolio.
The approach, he said, allows the recognition tools to be updated as Russian forces adapt their own methods, rather than relying on a static library of target imagery.
More than 1,500 drones produced each month
The scale of UKRSPECSYSTEMS’ wider operation has also increased considerably during the war. Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company now employs well over 4,000 people and is approaching 5,000, while producing more than 1,500 drones per month across its portfolio.
He declined to disclose the exact mix of aircraft making up that monthly output or how far production exceeded the 1,500 figure, citing operational security. The company says it is also working to much shorter development cycles than those normally associated with conventional defence programmes.
Chamberlain said hardware changes could be introduced approximately every three weeks, while software could be updated around every six weeks, with broader system updates occurring on roughly three-month cycles or faster. He said that pace was necessary because equipment that works effectively on the Ukrainian battlefield cannot be assumed to remain effective indefinitely as enemy tactics, electronic warfare and countermeasures evolve.
UK interest as exports begin to open
The public disclosure of RAM-2X also comes as UKRSPECSYSTEMS begins looking beyond Ukraine, with the gradual easing of Ukrainian defence export restrictions opening opportunities with NATO customers.
Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company is already seeing British interest and hopes ultimately to offer the capability to the British Army. He said: “So you know the Ukrainian export rules are starting to relax, and with the start of the drone deal, that means the export is open for those NATO customers, and obviously we have the UK showing interest, which is great, and we hope to bring this for the British Army.”
He added that there was also considerable interest elsewhere within NATO.
Commander calls RAM-2X a ‘game changer’
The commander of Ukraine’s 15th “Black Forest” Brigade, using the callsign Sarmat, whose formation has operational experience with the system, told us: “RAM-2X has been a game changer for the Ukrainian battlefield. For destroying HVT targets over 150km RAM-2X is the best.”
The unit price of RAM-2X has not been publicly disclosed, but the UK Defence Journal understands it is priced as a genuine consumable, allowing it to be employed in substantial numbers rather than treated like a scarce, high-end missile. We understand that a successful RAM-2X strike can in some circumstances destroy equipment valued at two to three orders of magnitude more than the cost of the UAV itself, and potentially four orders of magnitude at the upper end.
For context, the UK Defence Journal understands a P-18 Terek radar to be valued at around $3.6 million, an S-400 launcher at approximately $15 million and a Buk-M3 launcher at around $30 million. Those figures do not mean every RAM-2X sortie attacks equipment of that value, but illustrate the economics behind matching comparatively inexpensive precision-strike UAVs against high-value battlefield systems.
The comparison with conventional precision weapons is not exact, though. Different weapons have different ranges, payloads, survivability and target sets, but the underlying concept is to make precision strike affordable enough to be used repeatedly and replenished at wartime scale.
Chamberlain said this ability to change quickly was fundamental to the company’s approach, arguing that equipment has to remain relevant to battlefield conditions rather than simply meeting a fixed specification. He told the UK Defence Journal that UKRSPECSYSTEMS continually adapts its systems as operating conditions change, adding that the evidence of their performance was already visible in combat.
Why this all matters
Asked finally why he was personally so enthusiastic about RAM-2X and the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS approach, Chamberlain pointed less to any single specification than to the speed at which the system changes with the battlefield. He said: “You know, this is not, dare I say, a snake oil kind of scenario. The images are there. The reality is there.”
Larger changes, he said, come every few months or faster as Ukrainian units encounter new threats, tactics and countermeasures. Chamberlain said: “You have to be relevant on a battlefield to win a war.”
That, perhaps more than the 180km range or the numbers produced, is the point UKRSPECSYSTEMS is trying to make with RAM-2X. The aircraft being shown at MSPO is not a frozen design emerging from a development programme, but a weapon the company describes as shaped by combat, changed by combat and still changing with it.
RAM-2X is being displayed alongside the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS portfolio at MSPO in Poland from 8 to 11 September, marking the first time the company has been able to publicly connect its name to a strike system that it says has already spent years operating in the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Germany to Supply Ukraine with PAC-2 Patriot Missiles from Bundeswehr Stocks
articles.body:
Germany will supply Ukraine with PAC-2 interceptor missiles for Patriot SAM systems from Bundeswehr stocks.
Boris Pistorius, German Minister of Defense, stated this in an interview with Suspilne.
According to him, the decision was made at a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in light of Ukraine’s urgent need to strengthen its air defenses ahead of the winter season.
“I have decided to urgently provide Ukraine with the much-needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, in parallel with the NATO summit,” Pistorius said.
“Today’s second step with our partners on air defense: Germany is ready to support Ukraine with missiles for the Patriots,” Volodymyr Zelensky stated.
In addition, Germany plans to supply Ukraine with AIM-9 air-to-air missiles.
Pistorius also announced that Ukraine plans to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles. Their procurement is expected to be financed through the European Union’s defense loan for Ukraine.
Germany will also join the City Dome project, which aims to strengthen the protection of Ukrainian cities against Russian drones and missiles.
According to Tagesschau, Berlin is funding the purchase of tens of thousands of rounds of ammunition for Ukraine’s long-range artillery through a British consortium.
Germany has stepped up cooperation with Ukraine amid the August 4 incident at Leipzig Airport, where an FPV drone carrying explosives crashed near a Ukrainian An-124 Ruslan aircraft.
After identifying the involvement of Russian intelligence services in the sabotage, Germany began considering providing Ukraine with data from the country’s BND intelligence service, including precise coordinates for retaliatory strikes against targets in Russia.
Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI) also plans to establish a comprehensive set of measures to counter Russian sabotage, including cyberattacks.

articles.title: Sybiha, amid new Russian attacks, urges partners to boost air defense, weapons and sanctions
articles.body:
Following another round of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on international partners to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, increase weapons deliveries, and step up sanctions pressure on Russia.
"Russia should enter this winter knowing that the sky over Ukraine is getting harder to penetrate, that the missiles and drones it produces will be intercepted more and more often, and that the industry, technology, revenues and supply chains sustaining its attacks will face growing disruption and cost," Sybiha wrote on X.
He said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight, targeting cities and communities across the country with missiles and drones, with the attacks continuing into the morning.
"This is exactly what Russia does when it sees that repeated attacks carry too few consequences. It widens the geography and increases the frequency of strikes, testing how far it can go," the foreign minister said.
According to Sybiha, international partners need to make decisions now, including on additional air defense systems and interceptors, particularly to counter ballistic missiles.
Sybiha also called for providing more missiles for F-16s and additional aircraft to bolster Ukraine's ability to defend its skies, as well as for imposing tougher sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and sanctions-evasion networks.
"The world cannot stand idly by while Russia treats Ukrainians as targets on a shooting range," Sybiha said.
He stressed that closing Ukraine's skies should no longer be a matter of reacting to individual Russian attacks, but must instead involve depriving Russia of the confidence that it can keep terrorizing Ukraine indefinitely at an acceptable cost.
"The longer Moscow sees hesitation, the more it will try. The task is to change that calculation," the foreign minister concluded.

articles.title: Osa air defense missile stocks are running low, but Ukraine has developed the RK-19 as a replacement
articles.body:
At the MSPO 2026 arms exhibition in Poland, the Luch Design Bureau, part of the state conglomerate Ukroboronprom, presented the RK-19 surface-to-air missile for the Soviet-made Osa air defense systems and disclosed its specifications for the first time, Defense Express reports.
The Osa-AKM forms the backbone of Ukraine's remaining Soviet Osa fleet, and it is the missiles rather than the launchers that are running out, so a Ukrainian-built interceptor lets those launchers keep engaging jet drones and cruise missiles as the Soviet stock runs down.
Its maker's materials describe the RK-19 as designed to intercept subsonic and supersonic targets "at medium range," Defense Express reports. The missile uses radio-command guidance and proximity detonation and carries a 14.3-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The missile is similar to the original, but slightly faster
On its main specifications, the RK-19 is similar to the standard missile used by the Osa-AKM, although its maximum speed is somewhat higher, Defense Express notes. Both engage targets at ranges of up to 10 km and altitudes of up to 5 km.
However, their speeds differ: the upgraded missile reaches 600 m/s, while the standard 9M33M3 reaches 500 m/s. Their weights also differ: the transport-launch container with the new missile weighs 163 kg, compared with 157 kg for the standard missile, the outlet reports.
Domestic missile keeps Osa launchers firing at jet drones
The RK-19 will allow the older air defense systems to continue protecting Ukrainian skies and intercepting aerodynamic targets, including jet-powered drones and cruise missiles such as the Banderol, according to Defense Express. The price of the Ukrainian surface-to-air missile for the Osa systems and its production volumes have not yet been disclosed.
The Osa systems were effective through 2022 and into 2023, destroying a significant number of Russian drones and cruise missiles, Militarnyi notes. However, the stock of standard missiles for the Osa systems later began to run out, significantly reducing the intensity of their use, the outlet reports.
With interceptors limited, Ukraine's Armed Forces had to use older missiles for the Osa systems, which had poorer specifications, and integrated short-range air-to-air missiles such as the R-73. That route carried its own drawbacks: reduced range, and reliance on the missile's own seeker, Defense Express reports.

articles.title: Can Ukraine’s newly shown Koral become home-built answer to Patriot? Expert evaluates system displayed at Poland’s MSPO expo
articles.body:
Ukraine's newly shown Koral missile could become a home-built answer to the Patriot in addition to the "Freya" project. However, the system has yet to prove it can stop Russian ballistic missiles, Ivan Kyrychevsky, an arms expert at Defense Express and a soldier in the 413th REID regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on a YouTube broadcast.
Currently, the PAC-3 version of the Patriot is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal that reliably stops Russia's maneuvering Iskander ballistic missiles, and its interceptors are scarce, costly, and rationed for Ukraine by the US.
But in the podcast, Kyrychevsky places Koral, on the data available so far, at roughly the older PAC-2 level. A PAC-2-class interceptor can handle aircraft and simpler ballistic targets, yet it is not the ideal tool against the fast, maneuvering Iskander and Kinzhal that do the most damage. That leaves Koral a hedge against dependence, not a replacement.
The missile sits a tier below Patriot
Kyrychevsky based the judgment on photos released at the expo. The Koral missile lacks the gas-dynamic surfaces that would let it maneuver in flight, he said, and it carries a different warhead from the "hit-to-kill" round on the PAC-3. He did not treat that as disqualifying.
"We are in a situation where we do not just need means against ballistics, but means of at least some technological level," he said.
Cost tilts Ukraine toward its own missile
The economics push in the same direction. A PAC-3 interceptor runs about $10 million for export, and Kyrychevsky noted that even the US Army finds the missiles expensive to spend at the rate the fighting around Iran has demanded.
"We are better off building our own analog of the Patriot, even a mediocre one, than staying dependent on the regularity of external deliveries," he believes.
Winter still hinges on the Patriot
For all that, Kyrychevsky was blunt about the near term. Koral still needs to be tested against Russian ballistic missiles, even experimentally, to confirm its claimed performance, and power cuts at the plants that build it could slow production.
“My assessment for now is roughly this: hopefully, we’ll be able to put the ‘Koral’ to the test against Russian ballistic missiles on an experimental basis," he said.
This winter, he said, Ukraine will need Patriot interceptors regardless of whether it develops its own. Work on Koral began in 2016, and the system was first shown in 2021, a fast pace for a weapon of its kind, and a separate European project, Freya, is advancing on a parallel track.
In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine, in cooperation with other European countries, was working on an anti-ballistic missile defense system called “Freya". It is intended to serve as a cheaper and more widely deployable alternative to Patriot air defense systems.
Zelenskyy noted that, in theory, Ukraine could develop “Freya” on its own, but doing so would take significantly more time — potentially years. The system would require not only a missile and launcher, but also radars, command-and-control systems, and many other components. Even with European partners, the process will not be quick.

articles.title: UK brings forward maritime role for Protector drones
articles.body:
Britain is bringing forward plans to give the RAF’s Protector drone a maritime capability, with a review of the programme now under way and revised milestones expected by December 2026.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the move in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards integrating Protector with P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and Type 26 frigates.
Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan directed Maritime capabilities for the PROTECTOR RG Mk1 be brought forward, and a review of PROTECTOR is therefore currently underway. Rebaselined milestones are expected by December 2026, with a Review Note to follow.”
He added: “In the interim the Capability Sponsor, Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, is progressing capability development activity.”
The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended exploring a maritime surveillance capability for Protector, integrated with the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon fleet and the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates.
The review said Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance equipment and improved connectivity to give the long-endurance remotely piloted aircraft wider utility. It also placed Protector within the planned evolution of Britain’s anti-submarine warfare force under Atlantic Bastion, envisaging underwater, surface and airborne drones operating alongside Type 26 frigates, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The concept would use Protector’s endurance to provide persistent surveillance over large maritime areas while connecting its sensor picture with crewed aircraft and warships. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, providing a potentially useful means of maintaining coverage without continuously committing a P-8 to the same task.
The concept is not entirely new to British forces, of course. In 2021, a maritime-configured MQ-9B SeaGuardian, the maritime variant of the aircraft family on which Protector is based, took part in a series of demonstrations in the UK.
During Exercise Joint Warrior, SeaGuardian operated with an RAF P-8 in a manned-unmanned teaming demonstration supporting anti-submarine warfare activity, including the tracking, monitoring and reporting of sonobuoys.
The maritime MQ-9B configuration demonstrated at the time included a maritime surface-search radar, Automatic Identification System receiver and electro-optical and infrared sensors. General Atomics has also developed an anti-submarine warfare mission kit capable of working with sonobuoys.
Those capabilities should not be taken as confirmation of the final equipment fit for British Protector aircraft, which has yet to be disclosed or properly evaluated.
Defence had already begun examining a wider maritime role before publication of the Strategic Defence Review. In January 2025, ministers said Britain was working with the NATO Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Force to scope options for using Protector in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
After the Strategic Defence Review, however, the Government stopped short of giving a timetable. Asked in October 2025 when Protector would be integrated with P-8 Poseidon and Type 26, Pollard said the maritime capability was being considered through the forthcoming Defence Investment Plan.
The published Investment Plan subsequently allocated £590 million to Protector over the four years to 2029-30, but did not explicitly describe the maritime surveillance programme. It separately committed £260 million to upgrade the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon aircraft and equip them with the UK-built Sting Ray torpedo.
The latest answer now confirms that the Investment Plan actually resulted in a direction to bring Protector’s maritime capabilities forward, with detailed programme milestones being reconsidered as part of the wider Protector review.
That review comes as the overall aircraft programme works through a number of outstanding issues. The latest government major-projects assessment rated Protector Red, citing its pending programme rebaseline alongside trained crew numbers, Full Motion Video metadata dissemination and delays to weapons testing.
Some of those issues have since moved forward. Protector is already being employed operationally, Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026 and Brimstone 3 testing has progressed to analysis ahead of operational clearance.
By December, Defence now expects to have rebaselined the milestones governing the programme, including the work intended to turn Protector from a predominantly land-focused persistent surveillance and strike aircraft into another sensor within Britain’s increasingly integrated North Atlantic maritime force.

articles.title: Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers (VIDEOS)
Iranian forces have struck eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and targeted two US Navy vessels in retaliation for attacks on Iranian shipping, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday. It claimed the strikes inflicted “significant damage” on the ships.
US Central Command later rejected the claim that American warships were hit, saying, “no US Navy warship has been struck” and all IRGC attacks failed. CENTCOM added that US forces destroyed ten Iranian tankers over the past week, describing the vessels as part of a multi-billion-dollar network funding the IRGC.
The IRGC said it also targeted ten other ships that allegedly attempted, with US military support, to pass through an area of the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran declared prohibited and unsafe. The IRGC said it remains in control of shipping through the strategic waterway. The claims have not been independently verified, and there has been no immediate US confirmation of damage to the vessels.
The attacks came after the IRGC Navy issued an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of Bahrain and Kuwait to immediately abandon their ships.
“We warn all crew members of the tankers in the vicinity of the docks of Kuwait and Bahrain... to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the docks, as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy Command said.
The statement accused Bahrain and Kuwait of hosting US forces and being “partners” in Washington’s attacks on Iranian shipping.
Additional footage of a PATRIOT battery conducting a massive ballistic missile engagement over Jordan tonight. 
Well over a dozen interceptors can be seen engaging incoming Iranian ballistic missiles. pic.twitter.com/u69lJKtFJ7
Iranian retaliation began shortly afterward, with numerous videos circulating online showing ballistic missiles being launched from locations across Iran toward US military facilities in the region.
Videos from Jordan appear to show intense air-defense activity, with Patriot interceptors engaging incoming projectiles, including what some OSINT accounts identified as medium-range ballistic missiles equipped with cluster warheads.
Multiple OSINT accounts identified Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a major facility used by US forces east of Amman, as one of the principal targets. Some reported missile impacts near the base, but neither the impacts nor the type of warheads used have been officially confirmed.
US Central Command said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC allegedly targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the previous two days. The command said four tankers were struck in the Gulf of Oman and a fifth near Kharg Island, adding that US forces ordered their crews to abandon ship before the vessels were rendered inoperable.
The latest attacks follow another round on Saturday in which US Central Command said it struck three Iranian crude carriers after ballistic missiles were fired toward a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. Two tankers were disabled and a third, which was carrying no oil, was destroyed after the crew was ordered to abandon ship.
Iran subsequently claimed that it struck three tankers traveling along what it described as an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three US-linked vessels elsewhere.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the six-month conflict. The US maintains a naval blockade restricting traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Iran has imposed its own controls over passage through Hormuz and recently announced plans for an additional restricted maritime zone in the Persian Gulf.
Around one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, making threats to commercial shipping particularly sensitive for energy markets. Oil prices continue to climb, with Brent breaking above $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time in nearly two months as markets price in growing risks to global energy supplies.

articles.title: Despite Russian strikes, Ukraine’s BTR-4 maker built 600 vehicles
articles.body:
- Ukraine's KhKBM has built more than 600 BTR-4 armored personnel carriers since the 2022 invasion, with capacity for about 200 a year.
- The state currently has no active contract for new BTR-4Es, though the company has parts in stock for 100 to 200 more vehicles.
A Ukrainian armored vehicle maker has built more than 600 BTR-4 troop carriers since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, working through repeated missile strikes on the country’s defense industry.
The Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau, known as KhKBM, disclosed the production figure to a Militarnyi correspondent at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
The company relocated its operations after the 2022 invasion put its home city of Kharkiv within range of Russian strikes, and it has kept building the eight-wheeled BTR-4 armored personnel carrier throughout the war.
KhKBM says it can build about 200 BTR-4s a year at current capacity. The vehicle’s BTR-4E variant is roughly 80% Ukrainian-made by component count, according to the company representative, a level of domestic content that has let the plant keep working even as some imported parts became harder to source during the war.
Despite that output, the state currently has no active contract to buy more BTR-4Es, the KhKBM representative said. Militarnyi first reported the funding gap in June, when plant workers said they were finishing the last government order on their production lines.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has not placed new armored vehicle orders since the start of 2026, according to earlier Militarnyi reporting, with procurement officials saying deliveries are continuing under contracts signed in prior years while the General Staff works out this year’s requirements. KhKBM says it has enough parts in stock to build another 100 to 200 vehicles even without a new order.
The company used MSPO to show an updated BTR-4E fitted with a rear ramp built to a specification the military requested, which KhKBM plans to make standard on future production vehicles. The armor meets NATO’s STANAG 4569 standard, with frontal protection rated to stop 12.7 mm armor-piercing incendiary rounds and side and rear armor rated against 7.62 mm rounds. Mine protection comes from layered armored plates rated to STANAG levels 3a and 3b, backed by an aramid anti-spall liner inside the hull.
The updated vehicle also carries slat armor around its perimeter and upper hull to defeat shaped-charge weapons, along with chain and rod curtains meant to counter loitering drones that wait above a target before striking. KhKBM has fitted the vehicle with a Ukrainian-made electronic warfare system and says it plans to eventually add an active protection system and additional anti-drone netting to both the hull and its gun turret.
The exhibited BTR-4 also carries a new turret called Topaz, which KhKBM said is still undergoing testing.

articles.title: Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
articles.body:
Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
The Russian frigate Admiral Essen, which was struck on the night of 8-9 September, was hit by a Ukrainian-made Neptune missile.
Source: Ukrainian Navy; a Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+
Details: Ukrainian forces attacked the Russian warship with a missile during a combined strike by Ukraine's defence forces involving units of the Unmanned Systems Forces, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and other elements of the Ukrainian military.
Quote from the Navy: "Navy personnel used a Neptune missile to hit the Admiral Essen frigate, a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles."
More details: OSINT project Exilenova+ posted a satellite image of the Russian base in the city of Novorossiysk following the overnight attack. DIU reported that the frigate's superstructure was hit.
For reference: The Admiral Essen is a Russian Project 11356R Burevestnik-class frigate, launched in 2014 and commissioned into Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The vessel took part in missile strikes on Syria in 2017 and has been involved in strikes on Ukraine since 2022. It is armed with 3M14 Kalibr cruise missiles, the Shtil-1 surface-to-air missile system and a 100mm A-190 gun.
The R-360 Neptune cruise missile is designed to destroy ships with a displacement of up to 5,000 tonnes and, like other missiles of its class, can be launched from land, surface and air platforms. In April 2022, a Neptune missile was used to sink the Russian cruiser Moskva.
In late 2025, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was also using the upgraded Long Neptune version. The Neptune-D system uses RK360L cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,000 km and a 260kg warhead. The missile is designed to strike both land and maritime targets.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces and the Unmanned Systems Forces struck a number of Russian military assets in Novorossiysk and Anapa on the night of 8-9 September. Confirmed hits included a Su-33 carrier-based fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, two Russian radars – a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar from an S-300/S-400 air defence system – near Gelendzhik, as well as the Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.

articles.title: Transferring Patriot missiles from European stocks to Ukraine not a systemic solution – Czech expert
articles.body:
Transferring Patriot missiles from European stocks to Ukraine not a systemic solution – Czech expert
Michal Smetana, Director at the Peace Research Center Prague and Associate Professor of International Studies at Charles University, said this in remarks to Ukrinform, commenting on a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"The United States is a key player when it comes to interceptors for Patriot systems. Without American supplies, it is practically clear that Ukraine will face a significant shortage of them this winter," the expert said.
Michal Smetana / Photo: Michal Smetana/Facebook
According to the expert, the transfer of some of their Patriot interceptor stocks by European countries to Ukraine could provide partial relief, "but it is not a systemic solution."
In the long term, Smetana believes, new and cheaper systems for defending against ballistic missiles need to be developed. In this regard, he mentioned the pan-European Freyja project.
"However, deploying it against Russian attacks is a medium-term prospect, and even under the most optimistic estimates, unfortunately, this will not be a solution for this winter in Ukraine," Smetana said.
He added Russia can be expected to try to exploit the situation and concentrate its ballistic attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the fall and winter.
As reported, a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group was held on September 8. During the meeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Ukraine needs 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from partners' existing stocks, 500 air-to-air missiles capable of countering cruise missiles, man-portable air defense systems and $2 billion for drones.
Lead photo: Bundeswehr

Michal Smetana, Director at the Peace Research Center Prague and Associate Professor of International Studies at Charles University, said this in remarks to Ukrinform, commenting on a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"The United States is a key player when it comes to interceptors for Patriot systems. Without American supplies, it is practically clear that Ukraine will face a significant shortage of them this winter," the expert said.
Michal Smetana / Photo: Michal Smetana/Facebook
According to the expert, the transfer of some of their Patriot interceptor stocks by European countries to Ukraine could provide partial relief, "but it is not a systemic solution."
In the long term, Smetana believes, new and cheaper systems for defending against ballistic missiles need to be developed. In this regard, he mentioned the pan-European Freyja project.
"However, deploying it against Russian attacks is a medium-term prospect, and even under the most optimistic estimates, unfortunately, this will not be a solution for this winter in Ukraine," Smetana said.
He added Russia can be expected to try to exploit the situation and concentrate its ballistic attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the fall and winter.
As reported, a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group was held on September 8. During the meeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Ukraine needs 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from partners' existing stocks, 500 air-to-air missiles capable of countering cruise missiles, man-portable air defense systems and $2 billion for drones.

articles.title: US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- World
US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
US-operated Patriot batteries may have fired roughly 60 interceptor missiles to counter an Iranian barrage of just 20 ballistic missiles over Jordan, highlighting the enormous ammunition demands involved in defending against sustained ballistic attacks, Defense Express reported on September 9.
Iran struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan overnight, a facility used by US forces. Jordanian authorities said air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming ballistic missiles, while two fell before reaching their intended targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage from the attack, however, provides an unusually revealing look at how intensely Patriot batteries were operating during the engagement.
Defense Express estimated from available videos that approximately 60 Patriot interceptors may have been launched during the defense. Claims circulating online that as many as 100 were fired appear exaggerated, the outlet noted.
Even the lower estimate would mean roughly three interceptors launched for every Iranian ballistic missile in the salvo, although the exact number of Patriot missiles fired has not been officially confirmed.
Defense Express described several Patriot batteries as effectively operating in a “machine-gun” mode as they attempted to defeat the incoming missiles.
Video from the attack also appears to show Iran using ballistic missiles carrying cluster submunitions, adding another layer of difficulty to the interception effort.
The scale of Patriot expenditure is particularly notable because the systems protecting the area are believed to be operated by US forces rather than Jordanian crews.
Jordan has never publicly declared Patriot systems as part of its own inventory. The United States, however, has deployed Patriot batteries in the country when necessary to defend US facilities and support Jordanian airspace protection.
That distinction matters, Defense Express noted.
Previous cases of unusually high Patriot interceptor consumption against Iranian ballistic attacks could potentially be explained by limited experience among foreign operators.
US air-defense personnel have already spent more than six months responding to repeated Iranian ballistic missile attacks against American military installations since the beginning of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.
The crews therefore have substantial practical experience with this particular threat environment.
If the estimate of roughly 60 Patriot interceptors is accurate, the September 9 engagement illustrates that high missile consumption may be an inherent feature of defending against modern ballistic salvos rather than simply a consequence of inexperienced operators.
For Ukraine, which relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, the episode also underscores a familiar problem: successful air defense can consume enormous quantities of some of the world’s most expensive and difficult-to-produce interceptors in a matter of minutes.
As Defense Express noted, the question is therefore not only whether Patriot can stop ballistic missiles, but how many interceptors must be available when a sustained barrage arrives.
Earlier, reports emerged that US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks.

articles.title: Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US restarts Ukraine deal efforts
articles.body:
Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US revives Ukraine peace efforts
The phone call comes after US special envoys travelled to Russia and Ukraine to discuss ‘a proposal to end the war’.
United States President Donald Trump has spoken by phone with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin as the White House ramps up efforts to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
On Tuesday, Yury Ushakov, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, described the two leaders as having a “constructive and quite frank” hour-long conversation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 3Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
- list 3 of 3At least five people killed in Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s Kyiv
According to Ushakov, Putin talked with Trump about the ongoing war in Ukraine and Russia’s plans to advance its military goals on the battlefield.
“An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation’s goals and tasks was given,” Ushakov said.
The adviser added that Putin pushed back against rising concern that Russia could launch future attacks in Europe, including on NATO members.
“It was underlined that we don’t have any aggressive plans regarding Europe,” Ushakov said.
The White House did not return Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the reported call.
The phone call comes just days after US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss what Trump has described as “a proposal to end the war”, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
Ushakov told reporters Putin and Trump “exchanged views on the outcome of the visits”, saying some “very good, worthwhile ideas” were presented.
After his Sunday meeting with the US envoys concluded, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for “allowing them to come” to Ukraine, despite the ongoing fighting, which was briefly paused for the negotiations.
“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said.
“To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.
The meetings, despite being lauded by all sides, appeared to produce no breakthrough on ending the fighting. After the brief weekend truce, both countries resumed strikes.
Officials in Ukraine said Russian attacks on Tuesday morning killed at least five civilians and wounded 25 others in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported three people killed in the Bryansk and Kursk regions, with 13 others wounded. Ukrainian attacks on Russian-annexed Crimea also killed approximately five people, according to local authorities.
The war began in February 2022, after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, considered the breadbasket of Europe.
Trump has made ending the war a priority of his second administration, pledging on the campaign trail that he could achieve a settlement within 24 hours.
He later backtracked on that claim, calling it an exaggeration. Faced with reports that certain US munitions stocks are dwindling, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine for putting a drain on the country’s missile supplies and finances — though critics point to US actions against Iran as a major factor.
While Trump has had a rocky relationship with Ukraine and its president, he has cultivated a close relationship with Putin, saying they went through “a hell of a lot” together.
Last year, Trump invited him to Alaska for his first visit on US soil since 2015.
The Trump administration has faced criticism for seeking to end the war in Ukraine without fully involving Ukrainian and European officials. Trump and Zelenskyy are expected to meet later in the month, according to Ukrainian officials.

articles.title: The World's Best Companies of 2026
articles.body:
The economy built around AI has continued to boom even as experts and leaders work to hammer out the technology's execution problem and debate the guardrails that should be put around it. Demand for AI chips remains strong, as Nvidia holds its top spot in TIME and Statista’s 2026 statistical ranking of the World’s Best Companies, highlighting top performing companies around the globe based on evaluations of employee satisfaction, revenue growth, and sustainability transparency. But new companies are also entering the scene as the AI boom reaches down the supply chain.
Companies like Wistron (no. 16), Lenovo (no. 51) and Zurich Insurance Group (no. 70) are new additions to the 2026 list. Major Nvidia supplier Wistron reports that the demand for its AI servers continues to exceed supply. The Taiwan-based manufacturing company recently opened a plant in Texas to ramp up production. Chinese computer company Lenovo, known for being a maker of devices like PCs, smartphones and tablets, saw annual profits rise to record sales driven by the newer AI server part of their business. And the wave of growing demand for physical infrastructure to support AI has created an opportunity for firms like Zurich Insurance Group to cash in on selling more data center construction-related insurance. Zurich plans to expand its dedicated insurance and risk management solution for large-scale data center projects soon into Europe and Latin America. S&P Global puts total insurable values for each data center at up to $30 billion per location.
Beyond AI, European defense technology companies are seeing cashflow as a result of European NATO allies committing in 2025 to spend a projected €800 billion on defense readiness by 2030. “The increased defense spending in Europe is actually one of the largest demand signals we have seen in generations,” says Hugues Lavandier, senior partner in McKinsey’s Aerospace & Defense Practice. A good portion of that spending is still going outside of Europe, but Lavandier “won't be surprised that we increasingly see more of that spend going to Europe for sovereignty reasons.” The war in Ukraine among other recent geopolitical tensions has shown Europe that the art of war fighting and the equipment needed is also changing. “The share of that money being spent on equipment is actually going up,” Lavandier says, especially on new technologies like drones and unmanned vehicles, and addressing technical challenges like navigation, electronic warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Traditional companies in the space like French defense electronics maker Thales (no. 22; up from no. 224 in 2025) and Italian defense and aerospace company Leonardo (no. 25; up from a no. 126 in 2025) are seeing uptick in orders. At the same time, “non-traditional players are entering into the field, especially as suppliers,” Lavandier says. “In particular, a number of automotive players have entered into the fray…sometimes even selling plants, making capacity available.” Thales, for example, recently announced a sovereign drone partnership with French carmaker Renault (no. 42). A number of new startups are also taking this opportunity to translate the investment into innovations, sometimes as standalone products or in partnership with other companies, similar to Anduril’s ventures in the U.S. For example, German drone-maker Quantum Systems, which is currently supplying armed forces in Ukraine, announced significant investment from German telecomm giant Deutsche Telekom (no. 7), which owns the T-mobile brand, and also announced a new partnership with Rheinmetall (no. 287) to co-create an anti-drone shield.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence strikes Kalibr missile carrier Admiral Essen again: details of Novorossiysk attack
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence strikes Kalibr missile carrier Admiral Essen again: details of Novorossiysk attack
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has reported that on the night of 8-9 September, operators from its Active Operations Department, as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other components of Ukraine's defence forces, struck infrastructure at the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk, as well as the Russian Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Details: The DIU reported that the strikes caused a fire on the superstructure of the Admiral Essen.
The Admiral Essen is a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russia regularly uses to attack civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Ukraine's defence forces have struck the missile carrier on several previous occasions.
The Security Service of Ukraine and Ukraine's defence forces struck the Russian frigate on the night of 1-2 March 2026. At the time, a Ukrainska Pravda source in the service said that the damaged vessel was unable to launch Kalibr missiles.
In August, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence and defence forces also struck the Russian missile carriers Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov, as well as the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Background:
- On the night of 8-9 September, monitoring Telegram channels reported that drones had attacked Novorossiysk, causing a fire at a fuel oil terminal.
- The mayor of Novorossiysk confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed it had been caused by falling debris. He did not name the facility that had been attacked or provide details about the extent of the damage or possible casualties.
- OSINT analysts reported that facilities at the port complex had been struck, damaging at least one tank at the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal.
- The terminal is one of the key facilities of the Novorossiysk transport hub and forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest port by cargo turnover.
- On the morning of 9 September, Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, confirmed that the naval base in Novorossiysk, Russia's Krasnodar Krai, had been struck overnight.
