articles.title: FSB opens treason case against Ruslan Sidiki, who is already serving 29 years for attacks on Russian military airfield and railway bombing
articles.body:
The Ryazan region branch of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has opened a new criminal case against Russian and Italian dual-citizen Ruslan Sidiki, who was sentenced in May 2025 to 29 years in prison for an attack on the Dyagilevo military airfield near the city of Ryazan, blowing up railway tracks, and preparing another act of sabotage.
The rights project Ogni Svobody (lit. “Fires of Freedom”) reported that Sidiki is now also being accused of treason. According to information obtained by The Insider, investigators accuse him of passing information to Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, carrying out sabotage in Kyiv’s interests, and transferring money through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance to support Ukraine’s armed forces. However, Sidiki’s alleged cooperation with Ukrainian military intelligence had already featured in his 2025 conviction, meaning some of the same alleged conduct that the FSB is now classifying as treason was already used to justify the 29-year sentence he is already serving.
In July 2023, Sidiki organized a drone attack on the Dyagilevo military airfield. Then, in November of that year, he blew up railway tracks in the Ryazan Region, derailing 19 cars of a freight train. He was also convicted of preparing another attack on the railway, though Sidiki denied involvement in that episode.
In May 2025, a court sentenced him to 29 years in prison. He is to serve the first nine years in a prison, a stricter form of incarceration under the Russian penal system, and the remaining 20 years in a high-security penal colony. On July 1, 2026, the Military Court of Appeal upheld the sentence.
After the judgment took effect, Sidiki was supposed to be transferred to prison. However, he is currently being held at Ryazan’s SIZO-1 pretrial detention center, where he was transferred in August from SIZO-2 in Ryazhsk. Ogni Svobody said the transfer to prison has now been delayed because of the new criminal case.
Under Russian law, treason can be punished by up to life imprisonment.
Sidiki holds both Russian and Italian citizenship. Franco Fausto Salamena, an assistant to the Italian consul in Russia, was in attendance during closing arguments and the announcement of Sidiki’s verdict in May 2025. Sidiki’s defense had also sought access for representatives of the Italian consulate.
After his arrest in November 2023, Sidiki said security officers tortured him in order to force a confession. He said he was beaten, subjected to electric shocks using a field telephone and a stun gun, suspended by his handcuffed arms, and threatened with sexualized violence.
When he was placed in a temporary detention facility (and later a pretrial detention center), medical staff documented numerous wounds, abrasions, hematomas, and bruises.
Russia’s Investigative Committee repeatedly refused to open a criminal case into the torture allegations. However, those decisions were later overturned by prosecutors and by senior officials in the regional branch of the Investigative Committee, and as of April 2026, an additional review of Sidiki’s allegations was still underway.
Sidiki’s lawyer, Igor Popovsky, had pushed for an investigation into the alleged torture. He obtained medical records documenting his client’s injuries, challenged the Investigative Committee’s refusals to open a case, and argued that Sidiki should be treated as a prisoner of war due to the fact that, according to the prosecution’s own version of events, he had acted in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence.
In May 2026, Popovsky was detained by the Russian authorities on suspicion of large-scale fraud.
Sidiki acknowledged carrying out the attack on the airfield and the railway bombing but disputed prosecutors’ classification of the acts as terrorism. He argued that the targets were military aircraft and railway infrastructure used for military logistics, rather than civilians, and that his aim was not to intimidate the population.
Sidiki also said he had been in contact with representatives of Ukrainian intelligence, but maintained that he chose the specific targets and methods of attack himself.

articles.title: Will it kill off humanity? Computer scientists and politicians wrestle with risks of AI
articles.body:
Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?
These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.
Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.
Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”
The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).
On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.
Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.
Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”
The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.
Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”
The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.
Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”
On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.
The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”
ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.
Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.
He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”
Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.
The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”
Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.
Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”
David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.
“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.
“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”
Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.
“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”
Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.
“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

articles.title: Vietnam’s Communist Leader Meets With Putin in Kremlin
articles.body:
Russia and Vietnam signed a framework agreement Wednesday to cooperate on establishing a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam, as the two countries moved to deepen energy ties during President To Lam’s visit to Moscow.
Following talks with To Lam, President Vladimir Putin also said Russia was working to introduce visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens “in the near future,” though he gave no timetable.
Vietnam’s Deputy Foreign Minister Le Thi Thu Hang previously said Hanoi expected a “breakthrough” in Russian-Vietnamese oil, gas and nuclear power cooperation.
To Lam, who last visited Moscow in May 2025 to attend the Victory Day parade on Red Square and sign a strategic partnership agreement with Russia, held a joint press briefing with Putin after talks between Vietnamese and Russian officials.
In addition, Putin and To Lam presided over the formal launch of a joint infectious disease research laboratory via video link.
During his three-day state visit to Moscow, which began Monday, To Lam has so far met with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev and upper-house Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matvienko.
To Lam also met with Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, Russian war veterans and members of the Vietnamese diaspora at the embassy in Moscow, where he emphasized Vietnam’s transition toward diversified international integration.
Russia remains Vietnam’s top arms supplier and is involved in nuclear power and South China Sea gas projects, including in waters also claimed by China, though Hanoi has been diversifying its military sourcing.

articles.title: Oil terminal ablaze and four dead in Novorossiysk, two dead at Moldova border crossing in Ukraine as Moscow and Kyiv exchange drone strikes
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone strikes overnight into Sept. 9. In the Russian Black Sea city of Novorossiysk, a Ukrainian attack killed four people, including a child, and injured 29 others, according to local authorities. In Ukraine, Russian drones struck several targets, including a border crossing with Moldova, where two people were killed.
Krasnodar governor Veniamin Kondratyev reported that three of the 29 injured in the strike on Novorossiysk were in serious condition. Three private homes and five apartment buildings were damaged, along with an Orthodox church and a kindergarten.
In Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three more private homes and a kindergarten. No injuries were reported there. Damage from the attack was also recorded in the Krymsk and Temryuk districts.
Several industrial sites in Novorossiysk caught fire during the attack. The independent outlet Astra used footage posted by witnesses to geolocate the blaze to the grounds of the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal. The facility is part of the Novorossiysk transport hub and handles the transshipment of petroleum products.
Satellite data from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) also showed a fire in the area of the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal. According to its map, heat signatures were recorded near the terminal between 2:05 a.m. and 3:45 a.m. Moscow time on Sept. 9, with the strongest readings at 3:45 a.m.
The fire radiative power (FRP) in the terminal area reached between 25 and 27 megawatts, a level consistent with a noticeable fire, though FIRMS data alone cannot establish exactly what was burning or the size of the blaze. The system records heat anomalies, while the location of the readings near the fuel oil terminal provides additional support for Astra’s geolocation of the fire.
Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out a coordinated strike overnight on the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk. He claimed that several military vessels, including missile-carrying ships, were damaged or destroyed.
Brovdi also said Ukrainian drones destroyed a Su-33 carrier-based fighter jet, a Mi-8 helicopter, and two radar systems in the city of Anapa. According to him, the radars were a Kasta-2E2 system and a 92N6 radar used with S-300 and S-400 air defense systems in the Gelendzhik area.

articles.title: “We found the key to the Russians”: Ex-Defense Minister Fedorov returns from the US, planning Ukraine’s largest venture fund for defense tech and war think tank
articles.body:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has returned to Kyiv after a trip to the US and shared the results of his meetings. He announced plans to establish a major venture fund for Defense Tech in Ukraine and launch a think tank to help forecast how the war will evolve.
As defense minister, Fedorov drove Ukraine's shift toward drones, robotics, and data in warfare. His firing in July set off the rare wartime protests that reshaped the military's top command.
The fund targets military startups
The fund will be based in Kyiv and invest in defense technology, Fedorov said, backing not only new military startups but established companies that can scale their systems. He credited contacts built around the US firm Palantir, a tech giant whose clients include the CIA, FBI, Pentagon, and the US military, with helping him raise the resources.
In 2023–2024, Palantir signed memorandums of understanding with Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation, Ministry of Education and Science, and Ministry of Economy.
"I've published information about Palantir, and we managed to attract resources that will let us create in Ukraine, in Kyiv, the largest venture fund in the defense-tech direction," Fedorov said.
The company’s products are already helping Ukraine in wartime in areas including security, education, reconstruction, and demining.
He did not disclose the fund's name, its size, or a firm launch date.
A center would forecast Russia's moves
The second project is an analytical center meant to study the war rather than react to it. Its task, Fedorov said, would be to map Russian weaknesses and anticipate Moscow's next steps.
"Over the last seven or eight months, we found the key to the Russians: how to find their vulnerabilities, how to strike and seize the initiative in the sky and on the ground," he said.
Fedorov argued that Ukraine should forecast the war's next moves and prepare solutions in advance rather than only respond.

articles.title: Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe | José Andrés
articles.body:
In times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements for almost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.
Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.
In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least 1,010 humanitarian workers had died in 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.
“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who were killed by the IDF in April 2024 despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.
At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures. It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.
However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last month not to open a criminal investigation into the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic of guilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?
It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.
The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.
David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.
We might be numb to the sight of Russia disregarding our values. But we surely cannot tolerate the only democracy in the Middle East behaving the same way.
- 
  José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, and a Michelin-starred chef

articles.title: What Did US Envoys Achieve in Moscow and Kyiv?
articles.body:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky in Kyiv on the weekend to discuss how to end the war between the two countries. Afterwards, Witkoff called on both sides to make compromises. Zelensky said that security and economic guarantees for Ukraine had been discussed. Moscow described the talks as “extremely frank” and “constructive”.
Washington has embarassed itself again
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The visit to Moscow on Saturday was a diplomatic faux pas, rants journalist Edward Lucas (Lithuania) in Delfi:
“We should have been shocked by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff’s repugnant fawning over Putin. And also by the fact that Witkoff and his equally unimpressive sidekick, Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, travelled in a convoy of Russian government vehicles and relied on an interpreter from the Kremlin during the Moscow meeting. Unfortunately, repugnant rhetoric and actions from Washington seem to have become the norm. ... Much like the US president’s daily tirades on social media, unpleasant episodes only shock us until they are overshadowed by the next alarming piece of news.”
Time is on Putin’s side
Journalist and former deputy minister for infrastructure Mustafa Nayyem (Ukraine) analyses the situation on Facebook:
“Donald Trump has made his ability to bring wars to a swift end an integral part of his political image. Furthermore, the political calendar is piling on the pressure: the mid-term elections are just around the corner and the presidential election campaign begins about a year from now. ... The more urgently Washington needs results, the more sense it makes for Moscow to play for time, continue the war and wait for the next offer. This is why I would focus less on the number of visits by Witkoff and instead ask what has changed in Putin’s calculations after each of these visits. Right now the answer seems to be pretty clear: nothing.”
Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions
At least a functioning channel of communication
This diplomatic initiative must be taken seriously, political scientist Bernardo Ivo Cruz urges in Diário de Noticias (Portugal):
“The EU and Kyiv’s allies have made it clear: only Ukraine will decide the terms for ending the war. This means that we may have to accept a settlement that is acceptable to the Ukrainians but which results in tangible gains for Russia. An imperfect peace that would neither fully restore the justice violated by the aggression nor wholly uphold international law. ... Yet after four and a half years of war, the mere return of a diplomacy capable of engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv must be taken seriously.”
Too early for diplomacy
Diplomacy can only begin once Russia has lost, Le Point (France) argues:
“At this stage there will be no diplomatic solution to this war. Some conflicts end around a negotiating table. But there are others where the negotiating table only comes into play once an imperialist regime has realised that it has lost. That was the case with Germany in 1945. And with Serbia in 1995. And it is exactly what will happen with Russia too: the diplomats will only get to work once the reality of the battlefield has, in one way or another, been acknowledged in the Kremlin’s inner circles. Until then, the winter will be brutal, and we must help Ukraine to hold out.”
A small step in the right direction
Military expert Oleksiy Kopytko (Russia) is optimistic in a Telegram post republished by Echo:
“There is no doubt that the path to genuine agreements will involve heavy-handed pressure. Right now it looks like the US is intent on exerting pressure primarily, or even exclusively, on Ukraine, because the country is heavily dependent on external support. With regard to Russia, only China could assume this role, but Beijing has yet to intervene. ... This round of negotiations will not lead to an immediate end to the war. That would take a miracle. ... But it is a small step in the right direction. I am confident that by winter serious attempts will be made to initiate genuine negotiations leading to a ceasefire.”
Putin’s final bid with Trump
So far Putin’s hopes regarding Trump have been dashed, Gazeta Wyborcza (Poland) concludes:
“Putin and his entourage had hoped that Trump would do for them the job they themselves are unable to do on the front line, and force the Ukrainians to hand over to the Russians what they demand but have been unable to secure despite heavy losses. ... That was their aim at the summit in Anchorage in August 2025, but it failed. ... Trump’s shelf life is coming to an end. It looks as though his fellow Republicans will suffer a defeat in the mid-term elections on 3 November and his hands will be tied by a hostile Congress. ... So if the Kremlin can still get anything out of him, it has to be now.”
No hope without concessions by Zelensky
In a Telegram post republished by Echo, journalist Fyodor Krasheninnikov (Russia) sees the Ukrainian president playing a key role:
“I am wholeheartedly in favour of ending the war as quickly as possible, but in September 2026 there is only one way this will be possible – namely, if Trump’s envoys persuade Zelensky to accept Putin’s humiliating and unjust terms. Should this prove impossible for Zelensky, talks is all there will be. To those who want to jump to conclusions about my stance and ask, ‘Well what do you propose?’ I say: I am not proposing anything. I am merely saying that the war will continue and there are no other options unless Zelensky is prepared to make concessions.”
Russia wants to eliminate the Ukrainian state
All Russia’s demands call into question Ukraine’s very existence, making concessions on Ukraine’s part practically impossible, argues journalist Vitali Portnikov on TSN (Ukraine) :
“Russia has a clear ambition: the elimination of Ukrainian statehood and the expulsion of a large part of the Ukrainian population from the territories in which they live. ... It will not seek a compromise with a nation whose statehood it seeks to eliminate. That is why, since 2014, there has been no alternative but to stand firm against it; there will be no other option in 2026, nor beyond that. ... What is at stake here is nothing less than the right of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people to an independent existence.”

articles.title: Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen war threatens Saudi oil lifeline through Red Sea
Renewed fighting in Yemen is threatening a crucial Red Sea oil route that has become increasingly important to Saudi Arabia amid severe disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthi forces have pushed towards government-held territory near Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have launched a multi-front counteroffensive, raising fears that the most serious fighting in the country since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 could develop into a wider war.
The strategic significance of the fighting has been magnified by the wider regional conflict.
The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz followed the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, which Tehran has responded to by severely restricting shipping through the waterway. The strikes, widely condemned as a violation of international law, have forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on alternative export routes bypassing the Gulf, including moving crude westwards towards the Red Sea.
Central to Saudi Arabia's efforts to bypass Hormuz is the East-West Pipeline, which carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields across the country to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu.
The Houthis have already sought to disrupt that route. In July, the group said it targeted crude oil supply and transport infrastructure linking eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu, as Riyadh increasingly relied on the pipeline to circumvent disruption in the Gulf.
Between March and mid-July, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandab were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025.
The Houthis, meanwhile, declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in July and have sought to expand their control towards the strategically vital strait.
Bab al-Mandab, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, carried around 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products per day in 2024, equivalent to around five percent of the global total.
The result is an increasingly dangerous convergence between Yemen's renewed civil war and the wider regional conflict.
While Hormuz remains severely disrupted, fighting is intensifying around the other major maritime entrance to the Arabian Peninsula.
Those fears grew further on Tuesday when the Houthis launched one of their largest attacks on Saudi Arabia in years, striking four southern cities with missiles and drones. The attacks targeted energy infrastructure in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, according to Saudi and Houthi officials.
Fires broke out at several oil facilities, and 73 people were wounded, including women and children. The Jizan refinery, situated on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, can process around 400,000 barrels of crude per day and forms part of the kingdom's western energy infrastructure.
Oil prices rose above $100 a barrel on Wednesday amid the renewed escalation and further US-Iran fighting around the Gulf.
Yemen's war returns
The battle over the Red Sea is unfolding amid the most serious escalation inside Yemen in four years.
More than 500 people have reportedly been killed in the latest fighting between Houthi and government-aligned forces, overwhelmingly combatants but including at least 29 civilians.
Thousands more have fled their homes, particularly around Taiz and Hodeidah on Yemen's western front.
The Houthis launched their latest offensive last week, seeking to advance towards Mocha and territory bordering Bab al-Mandab.
Saudi-backed government forces subsequently launched counteroffensives across several provinces, with Yemen's internationally recognised government saying it ultimately intends to retake all Houthi-controlled territory, including Sanaa.
The fighting continued into Wednesday, when Houthi-run Al Masirah television said Saudi-backed forces had launched 32 airstrikes across Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah overnight.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed carrying out the strikes.
Houthi authorities have separately said at least 21 people were killed in strikes in Al-Jawf over the past two days.
The Houthis said Tuesday's attacks on Saudi Arabia were retaliation for Saudi attacks inside Yemen, while Riyadh described the strikes as a dangerous escalation and vowed to take measures to deter further attacks.
Saudi Arabia led the military coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, launching a years-long bombing campaign and blockade that devastated Yemen's infrastructure and contributed to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The 2022 truce largely ended direct Saudi-Houthi hostilities and froze the country's front lines, but the latest escalation threatens to pull Riyadh back into a conflict it had spent years attempting to extricate itself from.
The regional war has also changed the strategic stakes.
The Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to attack Red Sea shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, while their latest ground offensive could give them greater strategic depth around Bab al-Mandab.
Recent reports have also pointed to increasing coordination between the Houthis and other Iran-aligned armed groups, including Iraqi factions, although the extent of Tehran's direct control over Houthi operations remains disputed.

articles.title: US forces destroyed 5 Iranian tankers after IRGC attacks on US Navy warship: CENTCOM
articles.body:
Rabia Iclal Turan
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
US forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Tuesday.
 
 
"The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it said in a statement.
In a separate post on the US social media platform X, CENTCOM said the Iranian tanker M/T Riesco sank in the Gulf of Oman after being destroyed by US forces in response to the attempted IRGC attacks.
CENTCOM released footage showing the vessel sinking, saying it was destroyed on Sept. 8.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Tuesday that Iran would continue to lose tankers for every attempt it makes to strike US naval vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during his visit to Colombia.
Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that a tanker was struck near Kharg Island's anchorage area, with no casualties reported and the crew evacuated.
The state broadcaster IRIB separately reported that two oil tankers were attacked near the port of Jask, with their crews evacuated to shore by lifeboat.
The developments came amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz, despite the signing of a memorandum in June that envisioned a deal to reopen the strategic waterway as a prelude to a wider peace deal.

articles.title: Syria no longer under IAEA probe
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria no longer under UN nuclear watchdog IAEA probe
The UN nuclear watchdog's board of governors on Wednesday decided to close a long-time probe against Syria launched under ousted leader Bashar al-Assad after the country's new authorities led agency exports to key nuclear sites.
Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir al-Zour and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities. IAEA head Rafael Grossi said on Monday that a near-complete nuclear reactor found in Deir al-Zour and built secretly during the rule of al-Assad would have been able to produce material to make nuclear weapons.
The IAEA board "adopted by consensus" a text stating that a 2011 resolution finding Syria in non-compliance with its obligations was "terminated", noting the current government's cooperation, two diplomats told AFP.
The resolution, seen by AFP, was submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia and "encourages Syria to continue its cooperation with the agency, including the excavation work at the Deir al-Zour site".
It also "requests the director general to update the board, as appropriate, on the outcomes of ongoing activities of the agency" in Syria.
'Clandestine' activities
Assad was toppled in December 2024 and the current Islamist government came to power.
Grossi said on Monday that it was "obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine" activities.
Besides the reactor under construction at the Deir Ezzor site, the IAEA found a fuel fabrication plant where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured, and a location where nuclear fuel as well as uranium scrap and waste were stored.
In a confidential report seen by AFP last week, the IAEA said it found around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.
Grossi has praised Damascus's "courageous decision" to report the undisclosed site.
The UN atomic watchdog had declared in 2011 that the location was "very likely" to host a nuclear reactor, adding that its information suggested it was being built with North Korean assistance.
Last month, Grossi visited the site in Deir al-Zour in the east, which has been shut for 18 years.
In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secret air raid on the site 11 years earlier.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.
Israel also has an undeclared nuclear arsenal.
Robert Kelley, a former director of IAEA inspections and now an associate fellow of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told AFP following the IAEA report that there was "no evidence of any weapons programme" in Syria.
Instead the aim before the site was destroyed may have been to produce plutonium for North Korea, possibly to sell to a third party, he added.

articles.title: "Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
articles.body:
"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
Company commanders don't usually evacuate their soldiers personally. Their primary task is to direct their unit's actions from the command and observation post. But modern warfare has produced a rare breed of soldiers who are exceptions to the rule.
A few weeks ago, for instance, the whole of Ukraine witnessed how Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander with the 475th Separate Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), personally evacuated two wounded soldiers.
When a video was released of Polskyi running over to them with no helmet or body armour, dragging them off a broken-down unmanned ground vehicle and loading them onto a pickup truck, it drew thousands of admiring comments. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later awarded the courageous company commander the title of Hero of Ukraine and the Order of the Gold Star.
"It was brave," Eighteen says of Polskyi's actions. Eighteen, a company commander in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Regiment, says it is extremely rare for a company commander to take part in an evacuation personally.
Interestingly, however, at almost the same time as Vladyslav Polskyi was evacuating the two wounded soldiers, Eighteen also found himself in a situation where he could no longer stand back and direct the rescue of his men from afar.
Eighteen is 26 and has been at war since he was 19. He started out as a machine gunner with the 3rd Special Operations Forces Regiment, later serving as a marksman, sniper, squad commander and deputy group commander. He now commands a company in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment.
Recently one of his groups was on their way back from a mission when one soldier sustained a gunshot wound. Later, almost the whole group was hit by an improvised explosive device.
Four special forces soldiers were unable to walk independently, but ultimately all of them were evacuated.
Eighteen was, of course, far from the only hero in this successful rescue. The entire unit was involved in rescuing the group over the course of five days. The company commander is full of praise for the heroism and professionalism shown by all his comrades, from drone operators and medics to logistics personnel.
Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) has decided to tell the story from the perspective of Eighteen – a commander who would normally have been directing the evacuation, but this time went in himself to bring his men out.
"If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting"
It all happened in August, when a group of special forces soldiers led by a commander with the alias Santa, serving with the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment, was tasked with ambushing Russian troops along one of their routes.
The group infiltrated about 15 km into the area, where they succeeded in killing four Russians – they offered them the chance to surrender, but they refused. When the group received the order to withdraw, they moved into a forest to get some rest. But unbeknownst to them, danger was approaching.
"We were doing reconnaissance and spotted one of the enemy going into the forest where the guys were," Eighteen says. "He approached stealthily, and we didn't spot him until almost afterwards. We ordered the guys to clear the sector the enemy soldier had entered.
Just then one of our brothers-in-arms was shot and wounded. The group opened fire on the enemy and wounded him as well. We don't know what happened to him after that because the group was focused on evacuating our wounded brother-in-arms."
The bullets had hit a special forces soldier who goes by the alias Malyi (Little One): he had been shot in the abdomen and arm and several of his fingers had been blown off. He was given first aid. But then, as the group was leaving the wooded area, they triggered one of the improvised explosive devices that the grey zone is littered with.
By some miracle, Malyi wasn't hit by the blast – but now he wasn't the group's only casualty. Four other soldiers sustained severe leg injuries. One of them, Sava, died almost immediately after being dragged into cover.
Suddenly the group that had been evacuating one wounded soldier found itself having to evacuate almost half its members.
"The guys all had leg wounds," the company commander recalls. "There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic. They pulled everyone off the open ground and into the bushes so they could give them first aid, and they were treating the wounded, all of whom were now in a serious condition.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk."
Eighteen remained in contact with the group commander and watched everything unfold live. Heavyshot drones dropped everything that Santa's group would need for the rescue: additional stretchers and medical supplies.
"We understood that we couldn't leave the guys there. And time wasn't on their side – they'd already been in the area for about six days, and there were still around 13-14 km to cover during the evacuation. Everyone realised they wouldn't be able to get out on their own," he says.
Another group of special forces soldiers, which was on its way to a mission, was redirected to help the wounded. They evacuated one soldier, but the most seriously wounded man was still in the area.
Eighteen asked his commanding officer for permission to go in and retrieve him himself. He took a medic and two soldiers from his company with him. They managed to drive part of the way, but there was still around 15 km to walk.
They had to get to Malyi and carry him out without being spotted by Russian drones – and they did it.
"The most important things here are physical fitness and your knowledge. We got there as fast as we could," Eighteen recalls. "We picked up the most seriously wounded soldier. The medic immediately treated him, and since we had additional medication with us, we patched him up…
The main thing was that they realised we were now in the same situation as them. The group commander said when he heard over the radio that we were in the area, he said: 'If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting.'"
"There were moments when he lost heart. He said: 'You don't need to carry me anywhere'"
Early in the morning, the group led by Eighteen set off. The wounded soldier remained conscious throughout. The soldiers made their way through forests, over hummocks and through wooded areas torn apart by guided aerial bombs, and every time they had to make a dash for it, it was agony for Malyi.
"He was, shall we say, a bit cranky because of his wound. He'd been hit in the abdomen, so he was in a lot of pain, and it wasn't always easy to move him. Sometimes we had to run with him, carry him, or drag him," Eighteen recalls.
Drones dropped water, food and medicine for the soldiers. Time was another enemy, as Malyi was in urgent need of medical attention. The group would only allow the wounded man to rest occasionally, letting him sleep for an hour or two after taking painkillers.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on.
Towards the end, when he realised there were only two or three kilometres to go, his attitude changed completely. We'd give him a cigarette and a swig of water from the bottle cap. And he started urging us on: 'Come on, let's get through here faster, let's not stop.' We were really surprised. We were exhausted by then and wanted to rest, and he was like: 'No, no, keep going,'" Eighteen says, smiling.
The journey with the wounded soldier took 15 hours. It wasn't until midnight that Malyi was handed over to the medics.
"It was a good thing we did the exfiltration so fast, because at the hospital we found out he didn't have much time left: his liver had been punctured," Eighteen says.
By this time, another group led by one of the battalion's senior sergeants was halfway there. Santa's group, whose members had been wounded, had also managed to make some progress, but they couldn't move very fast because the soldiers were exhausted. The wounded were moved out gradually: the tourniquets gave them a little leeway in terms of time.
"His family were very grateful that we brought his body back"
Eighteen's work wasn't over yet. As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the medics, the company commander decided they had to retrieve the body of the fallen soldier, Sava.
"He hadn't been with me all that long. He was a calm person – a really motivated, determined guy who wanted to get things done. He didn't have a wife or children, but he had a mother and a sister," the commander recalls.
To bring their brother-in-arms' body back, Eighteen, his two fellow soldiers and the medic set off once again into the area they had struggled so hard to get out of. In the course of rescuing the wounded and retrieving the fallen soldier's body, the group covered more than 50 km in total.
Sava was laid to rest in the city of Kryvyi Rih. He was 35.
"We've already buried him. His family were very grateful that we brought his body back," Eighteen says.
The rescue operation took five days. Everyone except Sava made it. Despite the severe injury to Malyi's arm, doctors managed to save it.
"The legs feed the wolf, as the saying goes. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us"
"We try to evacuate all our wounded," Eighteen says. Photo: 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment
During his seven years of service, Eighteen has fought on many of the hottest fronts: in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
He had to personally evacuate a comrade in 2023, when FPV drones were in use, but before enemy drones had begun to dominate the skies the way they do now.
A 23-year-old soldier in the group was seriously wounded: both his arms had been blown off and his legs were injured. Eighteen and the group quickly gave him first aid and handed him over for evacuation. Compared with the recent operation, it was a piece of cake. Evacuating soldiers is much more difficult now.
"Now the sky is completely controlled by drones – both ours and the enemy's. The hardest part is getting into an area and getting back out. When you're operating in the area, there's less chance of being wounded. We used to drive in, but now we have to go in on foot, carrying a huge amount of weight.
If you have a casualty, the entire mission comes to a halt. Everyone switches to getting the wounded soldier out. And if, as in our case, you have four people who can't walk, you have to deploy every resource you have.
That's what happened this time: everyone was involved. The UAV component was working, unmanned ground vehicles were delivering supplies, and the battalion- and regiment-level electronic warfare units were operating too, providing cover across the exposed areas we had to run through," the company commander recalls.
Although unmanned ground vehicles have come a long way, rescuing wounded soldiers from the most dangerous areas is still mostly up to their comrades, Eighteen explains.
Unmanned ground vehicles take on a significant share of the logistics, but where machines cannot cope, the human factor remains decisive.
"A person can squeeze through a narrow gap, make their way through bushes, or wait things out in the ruins of a building," Eighteen says. "An unmanned ground vehicle is much more vulnerable in those conditions: it can get stuck or simply be unable to get through. And the enemy usually monitors roads and bridges.
So when there's a wounded soldier in the area, you have to take the risk and carry him out yourself, because the enemy can just destroy an unmanned ground vehicle on difficult terrain. As the saying goes, the legs feed the wolf. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us. Our work depends on our legs."
When we ask Eighteen about the most memorable operations he has taken part in, he recalls Sievierodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Velyka Novosilka. But he says the recent mission to rescue the group was particularly special to him. In his view, the most important thing for a commander is to value his people.
"We try to evacuate all our wounded. Of course there are some situations where the circumstances make that impossible," he says.
"We try to retrieve the fallen, too. Because people are our greatest asset now."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Life (Zhyttia)
Translated by Myroslava Zavadska
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: Rubio says ‘roadmap’ for renewed Russia–Ukraine talks could emerge within weeks
articles.body:
Rubio says ‘roadmap’ for renewed Russia–Ukraine talks could emerge within weeks
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a “roadmap” for resuming direct talks between Russia and Ukraine could emerge within the next few weeks.
Rubio called the meetings between American mediators in Moscow and Kyiv “substantive,” saying “new ideas were bandied about, it’s a very difficult conflict.”
For now an extended period we haven’t seen much movement on either side in terms of their willingness to make accommodations, and both side have very bright red lines.
Rubio did not specify what exactly the “red lines” are for Moscow or Kyiv, nor did he offer any other details. He said he did not want to be “overly optimistic” but said he was “also not pessimistic”about the prospects for further negotiations.
U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow and then Kyiv over the past weekend, marking Washington’s return to the negotiating process as a mediator. Previous talks had broken off in February amid the U.S.–Israeli attack on Iran.
All participants offered cautiously positive assessments after the meetings. Most of the optimism centered on the possibility of returning to three-way talks, an idea both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov raised. Neither side’s comments suggested an end to hostilities was near.
More skeptical forecasts circulated unofficially. The Financial Times reported that the central issue remains the status of the Ukrainian-held part of the Donbas, with neither side willing to compromise on it. The Bloomberg news agency’s sources reported yesterday that Russia plans to intensify strikes on Ukraine over the winter and escalate hybrid attacks in Europe to undermine support for Kyiv. The outlet called serious negotiations “unlikely” before next year.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine counting on first tangible results from Freyja anti-ballistic missile program
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, together with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, held a meeting with the heads of defense companies from partner countries, during which the parties discussed the Freyja anti-ballistic missile program.
"The main topic was the FREYJA anti-ballistic program, which is capable of providing Europe with integrated protection against air threats thanks to the joint efforts of Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom," Zelenskyy said on his Telegram channel on Wednesday.
According to him, during a meeting with the leadership of FirePoint, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener та Leonardo, the parties agreed on tasks for political leaders and government officials, as well as separately for manufacturers and developers.
"We are looking forward to the first practical results. I am grateful to Norway for this meeting. Thank you to our partners for their willingness to work together. Defending European airspace is our shared cause," the president said.

articles.title: Russian Saboteur Detained in Romania, He Was Spying on Ukrainian Aircraft
articles.body:
Romania’s Intelligence Service (SRI) said it prevented a sabotage allegedly planned at the direction of Russian intelligence services.
SRI reported this in a press release.
As part of the operation, authorities detained a Russian citizen residing in Romania.
According to the agency, his Russian handlers tasked him with photographing and filming sites of strategic military interest.
In particular, these include communications facilities and military bases used by NATO allies, defense and national security institutions, and critical infrastructure.
In addition, the detainee had to capture a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft.
On August 4, a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator was found near a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 Ruslan cargo aircraft in Leipzig. The German government officially accused Russia of being behind the incident.
“The information obtained points to a pattern of activity similar to that of sabotage networks operating across Europe and coordinated by entities based in the Russian Federation,” Romania’s intelligence service noted.
The agency added that the Russian citizen had been under SRI surveillance since February 2026 and was the subject of a large-scale investigation into attempts to organize acts of sabotage in Romania.
Cooperation with international partners also helped prevent the sabotage attempt.
It was recently reported that overnight on September 1, Russian Shahed attack drones struck the Orlivka international ferry border crossing in Ukraine’s Odesa region on the Ukrainian-Romanian border.

articles.body:
Russian has lost over 1.5 million soldiers since 2022

articles.title: Ukrainian company presents Shershen air-defence system and R-120K surface-to-air missile at exhibition in Poland – photos
articles.body:
Ukrainian company presents Shershen air-defence system and R-120K surface-to-air missile at exhibition in Poland – photos
A company belonging to the Ukrainian Defence Industry Association NAUDI has presented the Shershen ("Hornet") multi-calibre surface-to-air missile system, armed with Western and Ukrainian-made missiles.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda learned about the new development at the MSPO-2026 exhibition in Poland.
Details: The developer has presented the first operational components of the new missile system, which consists of the Perun combat control vehicle, the Athena radar for detecting and tracking targets and four Borei launchers.
A key feature of the Shershen is its open architecture, which makes it possible to use existing air-to-air missiles from different manufacturers and allows third-party surveillance and guidance radars to be integrated.
The system is claimed to be capable of engaging aircraft, cruise missiles and drones at ranges of up to 25 kilometres and altitudes of up to 10,000 metres. The system's radar can detect targets within a radius of 85 km, while its number of engagement channels allows up to six launched missiles to be guided towards targets simultaneously.
"At present, we can launch R-27, R-73, AIM-9 and AIM-132 missiles, and we can also try the R-60. Any air-to-air missiles with semi-active radar or infrared homing heads."
The system on display is the second operational prototype and is close to its production configuration. It has successfully completed the initial stages of testing, including shooting down targets at a testing range.
The launcher is loaded with the Ukrainian R-120K air-to-air missile. It is equipped with a radar homing seeker and can be used both from aircraft and by ground-based air-defence systems. The missile is currently undergoing design work, including development of its rocket motor.
Background: At the same exhibition, the Ukrainian Luch Design Bureau presented the RK-19 missile, developed for Osa air-defence systems. The bureau also unveiled for the first time the RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile, developed on the basis of the Barrier anti-tank missile.

articles.title: Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints
articles.body:
The Department of the Air Force’s new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s directives, redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints.
Unveiled 11 months after Hegseth directed changes to the Pentagon’s Equal Opportunity and Military Equal Opportunity programs, the new rules are dated July 28, but weren’t announced until late August. Hegseth called for the overhaul nearly a year ago, saying the programs had been “weaponized” by poor performers against leaders and commanders.
“No more frivolous complaints, no more anonymous complaints, no more repeat complaints, no more smearing reputations, no more endless waiting, no more legal limbo, no more side-tracking careers, no more walking on eggshells,” Hegseth said last Sept. 30 at an all-call with hundreds of generals and admirals.
The Department of the Air Force policy follows on similar updates from the Army and Navy, also announced in August.
New Definitions
Each military department’s policy includes the same new definitions of three key terms: “bullying,” “hazing,” and “harassment.”
The new definition of harassment represents the biggest change, said retired Lt. Col. Colby Volkey, a former Marine Corps Judge Advocate General. The new definition explicitly exempts standard training programs, stating “official military or governmental activities conducted in a professional manner, such as basic military training, professional military education, physical training programs, disciplinary or corrective actions, or combat readiness exercises, do not constitute harassment.”
It also states that “behavior that is rude, ignorant, abrasive, or unkind, is not necessarily indicative of harassment, but may constitute harassment depending on the totality of the circumstances.”
The revisions appear to be “an attempt to limit the types of activities that are considered harassment, Volkey said in an email.
The new definition of hazing no longer includes the phrase “any form or initiations or congratulatory acts that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same,” language that was included in the past in an effort to stop the practice of pounding on newly earned rank or other insignia, such as aviators’ wings.
Equal Opportunity Definition Changes
Bullying
Bullying: As described in DoDI 1020.03, while not a form of prohibited harassment under equal opportunity (EO) law but is a prohibited form of conduct, bullying is a form of harassment that includes acts of aggression by service members or DoD civilian employees, with a nexus to military service, with the intent of harming a service member either physically or psychologically, without a proper military or other governmental purpose. Bullying may involve the singling out of an individual from his or her coworkers, or unit, for ridicule because he or she is considered different or weak. It often involves an imbalance of power between the aggressor and the victim. Bullying can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.
Bullying is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:
- Physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.
- Intimidating, teasing, or taunting another person.
- Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.
- Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning, or dangerous acts.
- Playing abusive or malicious tricks.
- Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.
- Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.
- Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.
- Degrading or damaging another’s property or reputation.
- Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of bullying.
Bullying does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., command-authorized physical training). Service members may be responsible for an act of bullying even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Bullying is prohibited in all circumstances and environments, including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.
Bullying (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves repetitive, intentional hurtful conduct by an individual or a group, which intimidates, humiliates, torments, isolates, degrades, exploits, controls, or creates a risk of mental, physical, or emotional distress or harm.
- Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical pain or injury.
- Berating or belittling a Service member’s duty performance, professional abilities, or personal attributes.
- Threatening, teasing, or taunting a Service member.
- Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverable.
- Excluding a Service member from work-related opportunities, information, or social activities.
- Posting malicious gossip, rumors, and lies on social media, sharing humiliating photos, or sending vicious text messages
Harassment
Harassment (Military): As described in DoDI 1020.03, conduct that is unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person, whether verbal or nonverbal, written, electronic, or physical, that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment. Harassment may include offensive jokes, epithets, ridicule or mockery, insults or put-downs, displays of offensive objects or imagery, stereotyping, intimidating acts, veiled threats of violence, threatening or provoking remarks, racial or other slurs, derogatory remarks about a person’s accent, or displays of racially offensive symbols.
Types of harassment include, but are not limited to, discriminatory harassment, sexual harassment, hazing, bullying, stalking, revenge porn, and other sexual misconduct. Stalking, Revenge Porn, Other Sexual Misconduct. Formal complaints involving conduct that may be punishable under Articles 130 (stalking); 117a (wrongful broadcast or distribution of intimate visual images); and 120c (other sexual misconduct) of the UCMJ will be referred to the appropriate military criminal investigative organization or other law enforcement organization with criminal investigators who are specially trained to conduct such investigations. Harassment can be oral, written, or physical. Harassment can occur in person, through electronic communications, including social media, and other forms of communication. Activities or actions undertaken for a proper military or governmental purpose, such as combat survival training, making work assignments, or conducting performance counseling are generally not considered harassment. For the purpose of this publication, the DAF MEO program is limited to processing complaints alleging bullying and hazing as “other forms of harassment.”
Harassment (Military): Conduct by a Service member or civilian employee, without a legitimate military or governmental purpose, that would be unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person in the military environment, whether delivered verbally or nonverbally, including by written or electronic means, or in-person, that creates an intimidating, humiliating, or abusive environment.
Hazing
Hazing—As described in DoDI 1020.03, hazing is a form of harassment that includes conduct through which service members or DoD employees, without a proper military or other governmental purpose, but with a nexus to military service, physically or psychologically injure or create a risk of physical or psychological injury to service members for the purpose of: initiation into, admission into, affiliation with, change in status or position within, or continued membership in any military or DoD civilian organization. Hazing can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.
Hazing is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:
- Any form of initiation or congratulatory act that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.
- Pressing any object into another person’s skin, regardless of whether it pierces the skin, such as “pinning” or “tacking on” of rank insignia, aviator wings, jump wings, diver insignia, badges, medals, or any other object.
- Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.
- Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning or dangerous acts.
- Playing abusive or malicious tricks.
- Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.
- Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.
- Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.
- Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of hazing.
Hazing does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., administrative corrective measures, extra military instruction, or command-authorized physical training). Service members or DoD civilian employees may be responsible for an act of hazing, even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Hazing is prohibited in all circumstances and environments including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.
Hazing (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves intentional or reckless conduct by an individual or group, which humiliates, degrades, or creates mental, physical, or psychological injury or harm, or reasonably perceived as such, directly related to the affected Service member’s affiliation, entry, advancement, reinstatement, change in status or position, or continued standing within a military unit, command, or DoW or military affiliated organizations regardless of whether the affected Service member consented to the activity.
- Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical violence, including striking, restraining, branding, causing body modifications, tattooing, shaving, greasing, duct taping, or engaging in any form of unwanted physical contact that causes pain or injury.
- Subjecting a Service member to abusive physical discomfort or fatigue.
- Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverables.
- Requiring financial contributions.
Dismissing Complaints
The new policy instructs installation commanders to dismiss formal equal opportunity complaints in certain circumstances, such as if:
- The complaint “does not contain sufficient or actionable information to investigate.”
- “A complainant does not respond to request for information.”
- “A complainant files duplicative or related complaints”
- If a commander or supervisor to the service member making the complaint determines “through an adverse action or UCMJ action” that the complaint was a false official statement
Under the new policy, equal opportunity directors have five days to review a formal complaint before forwarding it to an installation commander, who in turn has 30 days to consult with the “servicing legal officer’ and determine if the complaint should be dismissed. The commander then has seven days to inform the complainant, who in turn has five days to appeal.
Giving commanders the power to dismiss complaints is a radical change, said David Sheldon, a former Navy JAG who now represents military clients from every service branch as a civilian attorney. The policy leaves it up to commanders to make a legal determination over whether the complaint is “sufficient or actionable.” Indeed, Congress only recently determined that commanders were not well suited to prosecute certain serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence.
“It’s kind of a step in the wrong direction in my thinking, for the very reason that you have a conflict of interest,” Sheldon said. Commanders have a built-in incentive not to be seen as having EO problems within their commands, he said.
Dismissing or resolving a case removes the holds that have sometimes delayed promotions, held key jobs opened, or resulted in foreshortened careers. Once closed, the policy states, “all favorable administrative personnel actions (e.g., awards, promotion, retirements) for an alleged offender of an [Military Equal Opportunity] complaint will be resumed or completed.”
Similarly, an individual being under investigation for an EO complaint is no longer sufficient grounds to withhold awards, promotions, retirement and other favorable actions. In the past, EO complaints have resulted in holds that could remain in place for months.
Anonymous Complaints vs. Confidential Reports
The new policy eliminates military equal opportunity complaints based on anonymous allegations, with some exceptions. Instead of filing anonymously, service members may submit “confidential reports,” revealing their identities only to equal opportunity directors and staff. But confidential reports do not constitute either informal or formal complaints, and therefore cannot trigger an investigation. Rather, they are merely a means for service members “to disclose allegations, receive information regarding available resources and reporting options, and obtain referrals to appropriate support services,” the policy states.
Commanders may choose to “look into the matter and take appropriate action in response to a referred anonymous report of prohibited discrimination or discriminatory harassment,” and a service member can choose, within time limits, to upgrade a confidential report into a complaint.
Allegations regarding sexual harassment and those concerning bullying or hazing are not covered by that limitation, however. Anonymous allegations regarding sexual harassment must be referred to the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response office. Allegations of bullying and harassment can be anonymous, but must include “sufficient information,” such as the offender’s name and rank, date of the incident, and units involved.
Shorter Timeline
The timeline for service members to file complaints is now shorter, just 60 days versus 90 days previously. But there are exceptions:
- Multiple incidents: In cases involving an alleged series of incidents or pattern of behavior, only one instance needs to have taken place within the past 60 days.
- Deployments: Service members who are deployed when an incident occurs and who lack resources at their deployed locations have 60 days to file once they return.
- Delays: Those who waited too long can submit a memo to their installation commander explaining the circumstances and seek an extension.
- Sexual harassment: By law, these complaints are exempt from the 60-day requirement.
A service member who makes a confidential complaint and then wants to formalize it, must do so within 60 days of the incident—not the report.
Sheldon suggested this makes it harder for complainants. Whether it is 45, 60, or 90 days, he said, “obviously “I would like a longer window just to give the aggrieved party an opportunity to be heard.”
Mediation
The new policy opens the door for “facilitation,” a form of mediation in which a neutral third party meets with the accused and the complainant to try to resolve the conflict. Facilitation is “a method for resolving problematic situations before they rise to the level of misconduct,” the policy states.
The confidential process can be offered for both informal and formal complaints, so long as both parties agree; commanders are instructed to consult with their legal offices before determining if it is a suitable solution for a given complaint. Commanders may also forgo facilitation if they determine it would “negatively impact good order and discipline.”

articles.title: Ukraine Develops Air Defense Missile for Desna System and Upgrades Strela-10 Systems
articles.body:
Ukroboronprom unveiled a new missile for the upgraded Strela-10 anti-aircraft missile systems and the new Desna systems.
This was reported by a Militarnyi correspondent covering the MSPO exhibition in Poland.
The RK-2PZ anti-aircraft missile was developed based on the Barrier anti-tank missile, which, in turn, is a modification of the R-2 missile family from the Luch Design Bureau.
The missile has a caliber of 130 mm, and the warhead weighs 6.1 kg.
After target acquisition, the operator selects a target for automatic tracking using a control panel via the television or thermal imaging channel of the optical sighting station.
The anti-aircraft missile is then launched from a launch container and guided using a laser guidance system.
A non-contact target sensor is activated as the missile approaches the target, and in the event of a direct hit, a contact sensor is triggered, initiating the high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The missile itself weighs 28.9 kg, and the missile in the container weighs 47 kg.
The missile is used on modified Strela-10 air defense systems, also known as Rif.
The Rif air defense system retains the MTLB chassis, the launcher’s rotating mechanism, and the operator’s station from its predecessor.
The system underwent its first live-fire tests in December 2021.
The Desna air defense missile system is a new module for the RK-2PZ missiles, mounted on a chassis that has not yet been demonstrated.
Currently, the specifications of the air defense missile system and its ammunition have not been publicly disclosed.
The Rif air defense system was first shown in service by soldiers of the 101st Separate Anti-Aircraft Missile Division of the 30th Marine Corps in June of this year.
