articles.title: Ukraine Unveils New 110-Km Vilkha Guided Missile With 220-Kg Warhead
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Unveils New 110-Km Vilkha Guided Missile With 220-Kg Warhead
Ukraine’s Luch Design Bureau has developed a new guided missile for the Vilkha rocket system, with a stated range of up to 110 kilometers and a 220-kilogram warhead. The weapon is currently in the final stage of testing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 9, the upgraded missile was presented at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland. The new 300-mm missile is 7.6 meters long and has a total weight of 907 kilograms.
The missile is designed to strike ground targets and adjusts its trajectory toward predetermined coordinates throughout its flight. Its guidance system combines satellite navigation with an onboard inertial navigation system.
According to Oboronka on September 8, representatives of Luch described the missile, designated R-624MS, as a further development of the Vilkha-M project. The new version has a maximum stated range of 110 kilometers.
The missile can be used with Vilkha launchers carrying either 12 or eight rounds. Oboronka reported that these could include existing 300-mm Smerch multiple-launch rocket systems as well as a newer eight-round launcher.
The new missile also differs significantly from earlier Vilkha-family designs. The previously used belt of 90 small gas-dynamic thrusters, which helped alter the missile’s flight vector, is no longer visible on the new version.
Instead, the R-624MS features a redesigned tail section with a rotating aerodynamic control assembly. According to Militarnyi, the new configuration allows the missile body itself to remain stabilized during flight, unlike earlier versions in which the entire missile rotated around its longitudinal axis.
Oboronka suggested that keeping the main body stable while only the tail assembly rotates could improve the continuity of satellite navigation and potentially increase accuracy. Luch has not disclosed further technical details about the missile.
The R-624MS is one of several missile projects recently presented by the Ukrainian defense industry. LUCH has also developed a new air defense missile based on technology from its Stugna missile family.
The new Vilkha missile is part of a broader push by Ukraine to expand domestically produced missile systems. Luch has also developed the RK-19 surface-to-air missile, designed to replace Soviet-made 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.

articles.title: 22-year-old Russian conscript sent to war despite suicide attempt. He went missing after an assault operation and was later declared dead.
articles.body:
22-year-old Russian conscript sent to war despite suicide attempt. He went missing after an assault operation and was later declared dead.
Alexander Korolkov, a 22-year-old conscript from Dmitrov, outside Moscow, was sent to fight in the war with Ukraine despite having attempted suicide during his military service, Veter reported after interviewing his mother.
Korolkov had been studying to become a food technologist at a vocational college when, in the summer of 2024, he took academic leave — and immediately received a summons from the local draft office. He was sent to serve, and a month later doctors diagnosed him with “mixed personality disorder.” At a training center for engineering troops in the Nizhny Novgorod region, he attempted to take his own life.
“I think it’s all because of the army, because Sasha is very kind, trusting, and sensitive. We didn’t have any problems like teenagers sometimes have, with partying or anything like that. He’s a very homebound boy. There, it seems, he couldn’t handle the pressure,” Maria Korolkova, the conscript’s mother, said.
After the training center, Korolkov was sent to a military unit in the town of Boguchar, in the Voronezh region, his mother said. There, he was admitted to a psychoneurological clinic and prescribed medication. She was assured he would not be deployed. But five days after his discharge from the clinic, Korolkov signed a contract for military service in Ukraine.
“We told Sasha that he absolutely should not sign a contract. Then he called me and said they had pushed him into it,” his mother said. The military unit refused to show her the contract, and she believes it was fabricated.
In April 2025, Korolkov’s unit sent him on an assault operation in the occupied territories of Ukraine. He went missing there, and in the summer of 2026, the unit petitioned a court to have him declared dead. His mother received a death certificate for her son.
